newsitem.title: JAPAN: Top Japanese prosecutor attacks media.
newsitem.headline: Top Japanese prosecutor attacks media.

text.p: Japan's new chief prosecutor criticised the media at his inaugural news conference on Thursday, saying sensationalised reports have hindered past investigations of major scandals.

"Recently, our investigations have become difficult because of news reports that jump the gun," Tokyo District Chief Prosecutor Tatsuhiro Ishikawa said. "Reports about people whom we have questioned have damaged the trust between investigators and the people we need information from."
Ishikawa said such reports have given rise to false theories that prosecutors were leaking information to the media.
Under Japan's law enforcement system, Ishikawa's office handles big, high-profile cases such as those involving politicians, bureaucrats and officials of big businesses.
In addition, his department decides which suspects will be indicted. Japan has no grand jury or jury system.
Japanese media often report about people being questioned by prosecutors, mostly because of the secrecy that surrounds their operations.
Such reports have been considered a breach of trust between prosecutors and the media. Some companies have been barred from official press events such as news conferences.

Ishikawa, the former head of Japan's "Untouchables," or the Special Investigating Team of the Tokyo District Prosecutor's Office, has handled dozens of high-profile bribery cases and other scandals involving top politicians.

They include the 1976 Lockheed payoffs scandal over bribes paid to Kakuei Tanaka, Japan's former prime minister to be arrested and tried in a bribery scandal, and the 1993 tax evasion case of Shin Kanemaru, the "kingmaker" of Japan's long-ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).
Both Tanaka and Kanemaru died while waiting for the courts to hand down final verdicts in their cases.
